events.title: The pass at the Caol mhòr steps
events.body: The Board's office begins issuing a small paper against a name, a face and a stated errand for anyone at Caol mhòr who means to leave the harbour road; the town takes to calling it simply the pass, and Martha Greaves comes to show her own to the same soldier three times that spring on Moot business.

events.title: Joe Ashby's boats searched again
events.body: A patrol captain boards every hull at Caol mhòr's harbour wall in the last week of an Cèitean, the engine-boats last and most carefully; Joe Ashby, watching from his shed door, tells him plainly that no guild in the harbour would give him leave to fit them, and the captain writes it down without comment.

events.title: Joe Ashby fits a fleet hull again
events.body: Before the summer is out the depot's own men send for Joe Ashby a second time, for a hull no guild-trained fitter at Seann Skell could put right; he mends it, takes his coin at the harbour's own rate, and asks no more of the matter than the coin requires.

events.title: The Moot's register adds the names of Àth leathan
events.body: Peter Hale brings Martha Greaves a list gathered from the western towns under the disarming; she enters the dead and maimed of Àth leathan into the Moot's register column by column, and finds Ruth Calder's own name on none of its three columns.

events.title: Easter kept under watch
events.body: Martha Greaves stands at the back of the Tuathaich Church's own Easter service at the chapel above Doire ghlas and finds a single soldier of the regiments posted at the door the whole length of it, writing nothing in his book, the service passing between door and altar without a word exchanged.

events.title: Ellen Marsh takes down the Cnoc thais women
events.body: In the schoolroom given over the autumn before, Ellen Marsh takes down the accounts of the women of Cnoc thais bench by bench for her twelfth book, among them Peggy Innes's telling of a farm that bakes a second loaf every night and leaves it on the sill for a coming and going the disarming never ended.

events.title: A hill farm burned above Cnoc thais
events.body: A patrol of the regiments finds a farm above Cnoc thais with a barn half full of grain no ration book can account for and burns the house and byre, turning the family into their own yard first; no one is killed, and Ellen Marsh sets the telling down in the same flat voice the women themselves use for it.

events.title: Ellen Marsh finishes her twelfth book
events.body: In the first week of an Dàmhair Ellen Marsh closes the twelfth of her books of Tuathaich accounts, the one that gathers the war her first eleven never spoke of, and writes on its last leaf that she does not know which of her twelve a reader two generations off will find the harder to believe.

events.title: The fourth regiment's year of patrols on the Ceann mhòr road
events.body: Through the whole quartered year the fourth regiment keeps its patrols on the Ceann mhòr road, a file out at first light and in at dusk; no arms and no unaccounted man are found, and the regiment's returns settle into the same three words that closed every report of the autumn before.

events.title: Dùghall hears the hymn through the wall
events.body: Of an evening in an t-Sultain, Dùghall mac Iain hears through the wall of Barbara's house a hymn sung low in the humans' tongue, heavier than her shuttle-song of the autumn before; by an Dàmhair he can carry its whole shape in his head without meaning to have learned it, and catches himself humming it on the road.

events.title: Cailean's own grandmother's tune
events.body: Dùghall mac Iain hums two bars of the learned hymn to the soldier Cailean over a cold supper; Cailean says his own grandmother kept a tune very like it, that he never asked its words either, and that a man billeted long enough on a house not his own generally carries some piece of it home in him.

events.title: A rumour that will not run to ground
events.body: Across the quartered year a single rumour passes from the Cnoc thais hill paths to the Doire ghlas schoolroom to the Ceann mhòr road, that something gathers in the western hills the disarming never reached; no regiment's patrol and no clerk's report ever explains it, and it never twice is told the same way.

events.title: Word reaches Caol mhòr that the hills are moving
events.body: In the last week of an Dàmhair a Board carrier rides two days without pausing to bring Caol mhòr word that some hundreds have come down out of the western hills and turned south-east across the middle of the island; Martha Greaves reads the note beside her register's own closed column on the names of Àth leathan.

events.title: A burial walked to on a pass
events.body: A carter of Caol mhòr shows his pass at the harbour steps in his mourning black to walk to his father's burial two roads inland, the office having made no separate provision for burials.

events.title: A byre-boy's raised hand
events.body: On the Ceann mhòr road a boy of ten driving three cows begins, in the second season of the patrols, to lift a hand to the fourth regiment's file as it passes.

events.title: Bread left on a sill above Cnoc thais
events.body: A farm two ridges back from ruined Cnoc thais bakes twice what its household can eat and leaves the second baking on the sill overnight; the loaves are gone by morning and the sill is never watched.

events.title: Goods carried out before the thatch was fired
events.body: Marion Kenny tells Ellen Marsh that the family of the burned farm above Cnoc thais were given time by the patrol to carry out a chest, a loom and the year's meal before the thatch was fired.

events.title: A Board clerk counts night traffic on the hill paths
events.body: A clerk of the Board stationed at Cnoc thais writes to the Moot that the hill paths above the town carry more foot-traffic by night than any patrol's daylight count can explain.

events.title: The passes printed at Cathair dhearg
events.body: The passes of the northern office are printed at Cathair dhearg on grey card, ten thousand at a time, with a space for a name and none for a trade.

events.title: Àth bheag's report of the ford
events.body: The maor of Àth bheag writes the fullest report of the column's road: some four hundred men forded the water below the bridge at dawn, in order, without banner or drum, and went on south without stopping.

events.title: Sìleas nic Rath keeps a file of the column's road
events.body: The royal chronicler asks every town on the column's line for its account and is given leave to keep them, a freedom the war itself never allowed her.

events.title: Bread bought and paid for at Muileann mhin
events.body: Two men of the column buy the widow Mòrag nic Fhearghais's whole morning's baking at Muileann mhin and pay in full before the company passes, taking nothing else from the town.

events.title: Muileann mhin's miller reports no loss
events.body: The miller of Muileann mhin under the western hills writes to the Board that the town's takings showed no loss by the column's passing, the bread having been paid for at a fair price and nobody's stock troubled beyond it.

events.title: A night's lodging paid at a barn on the capital's edge
events.body: A party of the column sleeps a night in Aonghas mac Cuinn's barn and leaves coin and a note under a stone, thanking him and asking nothing more.

events.title: The column keeps wide of the towns of the fair country
events.body: Crossing the open country toward the capital's fields, the column holds a road that passes no town of any size, and the small farms it crosses report only a quiet passing.

events.title: The fair-ground at Muileann òg ordered for the regiments
events.body: The first regiment's quartermaster requires the fair-ground, its booths and its cleared ground for the first and third regiments, over the fair court's own market set for the ninth.

events.title: Fionnlagh Dubh numbers his stall's timbers
events.body: An ironmonger of thirty years' standing at Muileann òg's fair chalks numbers on his stall's poles before stacking them, against a spring market neither he nor the clerk much believes will come.

events.title: The third regiment camps on the cleared fair-ground
events.body: The third regiment pitches its tents where the ironmonger's stall and the cheese-sellers' row stood the day before, the ground cleared from the toll-house arch to the river bend.

events.title: The first regiment fills Muileann òg
events.body: The first regiment comes down the same evening as the third and fills the fair-ground, the water-meadow and the lanes above the mill, so that Muileann òg holds more soldiers under canvas than people.

events.title: The fair court keeps its small business through the camp
events.body: Ùna nic Ailein keeps the fair court open through the regiments' camp, hearing a strayed cow and a firewood complaint while the road to Muileann ghlas fills and empties below her window.

events.title: Ùna nic Ailein's book closes with no entry
events.body: Unable to set a sum against a market that never ran, Ùna rules the line the court's form requires, leaves it blank, and closes the year the desk with no closing entry.

events.title: The maor of Àth bheag watches from the bank
events.body: Cailean mac Griogair, maor of Àth bheag, woken by the smith's boy, stands at the field's edge in a borrowed coat watching the column ford the water and does not go down to ask where it is bound.

events.title: No banner and no drum
events.body: The miller's wife of Àth bheag, watching the column cross from the mill loft, says she saw no banner among them and no drum, only a man at the head whom the rest left the whole width of the road.

events.title: Mòrag nic Fhearghais bakes through the morning
events.body: The widow baker of Muileann mhin under the western hills bakes through the morning with two daughters for the column, and enters the sale as bread to the western company, paid in full.

events.title: The note under the stone
events.body: Aonghas mac Cuinn finds under a stone on his barn floor coin for a week's rent and a note in Dia-thìris: for the barn, and thanks; we have asked nothing else. It is the only writing in the Library's file that can be set to a hand inside the column.

events.title: The eel-woman's tub carried off the fair-ground
events.body: Clearing the fair-ground at Muileann òg for the regiments, two soldiers lift the heavier end of the eel-woman's tub onto her handcart for her.

events.title: The column sings through its last night in the open
events.body: On the bank and in the thorn below Muileann ghlas the column keeps its last night before the battle by singing low, company after company, in part for what courage it lends and in part because there are children on the field with nowhere else on the island to be left.

events.title: Owen Barrow walks the line before first light
events.body: In the last hour of dark Owen Barrow goes the length of the column's line, speaking to each company and to many of the column by name; he is remembered in the north to have said that the hills lie behind them now and cannot be walked back to before the guns find them either way. The open record names him nowhere.

events.title: The guns find the thorn stand
events.body: The third regiment's four field pieces, hauled the last two miles by hand through ground too soft for the horses, find the column's thorn-stand line within the first half-hour of the fighting; what holds after that holds along the bank itself, hand to hand, through most of the short forenoon.

events.title: The corporal's list at the mill
events.body: A corporal of the third regiment draws up the regiments' dead of the day at a trestle table in the mill at Muileann ghlas, the miller's own ledger turned backward for want of other paper: three-and-twenty names, each with a town and, where known, an age.

events.title: A requisition for lime
events.body: The regiments' burial parties ask the quartermaster for a good deal more lime than three-and-twenty graves would need. The requisition survives where no count of the column's own dead does, and is the nearest thing the open record holds to one.

events.title: The miller's wife keeps her kitchen through the battle
events.body: As the mill at Muileann ghlas changes hands twice before noon, the miller's wife will not leave her own kitchen for either army, and is remembered by the regiments' surgeon to have gone on moving her pots and sacks from whichever corner the fighting had just left.

events.title: The colonel's report
events.body: The first regiment's colonel writes that the column held the bank at Muileann ghlas longer than any force he had faced in two years of war, and sets it down, he says, only so his council should have the field's truth and not a prettier account of it.

events.title: The taken ground remembered
events.body: An old man of Muileann ghlas, brought before the regiments' officers to answer for a store of grain, tells them the field carries an older name, the taken ground, from a battle of the Brothers' War fought on the same ground two centuries before.

events.title: The sixty come out of the byres
events.body: After dark, some sixty of the column still holding the mill and its byres come out under a promise, carried by a Tuathach prisoner on a white cloth, that any man unarmed will be marched and not shot; they are counted, searched and held overnight on the mill floor.

events.title: The regiments' surgeon treats both sides alike
events.body: The regiments' own surgeon, two years out of his training, tends the wounded of both the regiments and the column through the night at Muileann ghlas by two lanterns and a banked fire, and the open record notes that he made no distinction between them.

events.title: The old man of Cnoc thais brings down his cow
events.body: A lame old man of Cnoc thais comes down to the seventh regiment's northernmost post on the Àth leathan road carrying no weapon, leading on a rope halter the one cow his family kept through two summers of war, and is let through with it.

events.title: The sergeant judges the counting done
events.body: At the seventh regiment's northernmost post the sergeant keeping the list of the hills' people notes, when no one more has come down the road by noon, that he takes the empty road to mean the counting is finished.

events.title: Somhairle hears the guns are done
events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn hears at the capital, from a clerk who comes into his room without knocking, that the fighting at Muileann ghlas is over; he says afterward that his first thought was for the coal line's timetable and the wounded's carriage north.

events.title: Somhairle checks the wounded trains twice over
events.body: In the first weeks of the peace Somhairle mac Lachlainn has the coal line's schedule for the war's wounded checked twice against the surgeons' own returns, to be sure no man carried north that winter rode on a train meant for other cargo.

events.title: Four guns hauled the last two miles by hand
events.body: The third regiment's four guns come down from the capital by the coal line and are hauled the last two miles to the field at Muileann ghlas by hand, the ground too soft for horses.

events.title: The mill at Muileann ghlas changes hands twice
events.body: In the morning's fighting the mill at Muileann ghlas is taken by the column from a picket of the first regiment and taken back, the miller's wife moving her pots out of whatever corner the fighting last left.

events.title: The white cloth on a byre-fork
events.body: At dusk the first regiment's colonel sends word by a Tuathach prisoner under a white cloth on a byre-fork that any man who comes out unarmed will be marched, not shot, to the capital's gaol.

events.title: Near ninety of the column's wounded brought in
events.body: The regiments' surgeon's tally for the night after Muileann ghlas stands at twenty-three of the regiments buried or dying and near ninety of the column's wounded brought in.
